# Metrics

**Generated from `metrics.Catalogue()`. Do not edit — change the catalogue.**

The engine exports OpenTelemetry metrics through the same `OTEL_*` environment
its traces use, because a company has one telemetry backend and two settings
would let you split signals across two of them where a correlation resolves on
neither:

| Variable | What it does |
|---|---|
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | The collector. Metrics are posted to `<endpoint>/v1/metrics`. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT` | Overrides the base for metrics alone. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` | `http/protobuf` (default) or `grpc`. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` | Sent with every export — an API key, a tenant. |
| `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER` | `none` switches the export off and leaves traces on. |
| `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL` | Export period in milliseconds. Default 60000. |

**The provider is installed whether or not you are collecting.** Every
instrument exists either way, so no code path in the engine branches on
whether metrics are "on", and the numbers on `crewlet retention status` are
read from the same recorder a collector would be reading. With no endpoint set
the measurements are taken and not shipped.

**Every attribute below is a closed set.** No metric carries a task key, a
subject id, a page title or a node id as an attribute — the node is the
resource, set once — so the number of time series is bounded by this page
rather than by how much work your company has done.

## Histograms

A distribution, exported with the engine's own bucket boundaries, which are its unit's: in `ms`, 1, 2 and 5 times every power of ten from 10 µs to 5·10⁷ ms (nearly fourteen hours), so every budget an alarm holds a percentile to is a boundary and the alarm fires exactly past it; in `1`, the same series from 1 to 500 000; in `By`, every power of two from 1 KiB to 2 GiB. Each resolves a percentile to within a factor of two and a half at every scale its unit is recorded at, from a 40 µs index probe to a backup of hours and a push's bundle of a gibibyte. The SDK's default boundaries stop at 10 s, so a slow apply would land in an overflow bucket and read as "at least 10 s" for ever.

| Metric | Unit | Attributes | What it makes visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.duration` | `ms` | `domain`, `outcome` | A write path slowing down before it starts refusing. The outcome dimension separates the three answers a write has, so a rise in `pending` reads as an applier falling behind rather than as a broker getting slower. |
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.rounds` | `1` | `domain` | Contention on one subject, which the compare-and-set round cap bounds and nothing measured. A distribution creeping toward the cap is a hot object; reaching it is a refusal a model reads as a colleague editing the same thing. |
| `crewlet.statelog.write.session_wait` | `ms` | `domain` | The wait a write pays for its own previous write to apply. Zero when the caller is caught up, which is the common case, and the shape of the load that is not. |
| `crewlet.statelog.barrier.duration` | `ms` | `domain` | The broker round trip under every linearizable read, and the first number a drifting fsync or a degrading quorum moves. It was a benchmark's p50 on an idle loopback cluster and nothing in production. |
| `crewlet.statelog.read.wait` | `ms` | `domain`, `level` | How much of the read budget a barrier or session wait actually spends. A p95 approaching the budget is reads about to start refusing, which is the warning the refusal itself is too late to be. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.latency` | `ms` | `domain` | THE COMMIT-TO-APPLY GAP: from the broker's own timestamp on a record to this node committing it. Every read level is a policy about this quantity and nothing measured it. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.tx.duration` | `ms` | `domain`, `bound_by` | How long one apply transaction holds the store's writer, and which budget ended it. A transaction is what every waiter behind it pays, and rows were only ever a proxy for the duration. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.record.duration` | `ms` | `domain`, `kind` | One record's apply. A single record past the time budget is still one transaction, so this is the real ceiling on how long a read can be delayed — a sentence in a design document until it was measured. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.batch.rows` | `1` | `domain` | Rows per apply transaction, which is what the row budget bounds and what the drain rate divides. |
| `crewlet.backup.duration` | `ms` | — | How long a backup took, which is the window the trim hold covers and the I/O the copy spends competing with the applier's own commits. It is what turns the retention guide's worked example into a number for THIS hardware. |
| `crewlet.store.pool.wait` | `ms` | `file` | How long a reader waited for a connection. It is what says the reader pool is too small on this node, which nothing could say before. |
| `crewlet.tracker.search.scan.duration` | `ms` | `path`, `rung` | One search's scan, recorded by the node that coordinated it, split by what it ran for (`path`: `prefetch` for a turn's knowledge prefetch, which the turn waits on before its first token, `interactive` for somebody's deliberate search) and by the ranking it actually served (`rung`: hybrid, keyword, semantic, or none). Each path has its own budget — half a second for a prefetch (`prefetch_slow`), a second for an interactive search (`search_slow`) — and read as one series the quicker one hides the other; a keyword scan is a fraction of a fused one's cost, so reading rungs as one series hides a slow meaning half. |
| `crewlet.objects.s3.request.attempts` | `1` | `operation`, `outcome` | How many attempts each request of this node's S3 client took, observed once as it ends, by `operation` and how it ended (`outcome`): `answered` — the bucket's final answer, a success or a refusal; `given_up` — the bucket answered nothing but failures (server errors that are no throttle, or no answer at all) from the first to a bound drawn for it between forty seconds and a minute after it, or stopped moving one of its attempts for a minute (`stalled` on the attempts counter), so the request was not asked again and its caller was told the bucket's last answer; `ended` — its deadline or its caller ended it after at least one attempt, one still throttled among them; `unsent` — it ended before its first attempt, observed at zero: its deadline or its caller ended it while it waited at the gate (the gate starving the node's requests), or it was refused before sending; `failed` — a failure asking again cannot change, such as a certificate the node does not trust, or an S3 Express session that could not be had for it. Nothing counts a request's attempts but its deadline and that bound, so the tail is how long the bucket made requests wait: a p95 above one is a bucket throttling or failing, and `given_up` above zero is a bucket that failed every attempt for most of a minute, or held one for a whole minute without moving it. |
| `crewlet.code.commit.batch.size` | `1` | — | Pushes per code record: group commit working, or not. The committer takes everything already queued behind an in-flight record — without lingering for more — so an idle repository's records stay at one push and a busy one's grow, up to 64. A busy repository whose batches stay at one is one whose pushes arrive more slowly than a record commits. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.check.duration` | `ms` | `trigger` | How long one check of a copy's index files, or one scrub of every file it holds, took, by `trigger` (`first`, `unvouched`, `scrub`, `report`, `forced` or `request`, as `crewlet.code.cache.checks`), counted only where it read something. A check is what a copy's first request after a restart waited for beside its sync — about a quarter of the copy's pack bytes read; a scrub runs behind the serving and nobody waits for it, reading every byte the copy holds. Both hash on one core, a read slot a 64 MiB piece, and at the volume's own throughput when read cold. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.sync.duration` | `ms` | `kind` | How long a completed cache sync took, by `kind` (`delta`: the rows moved since the cache's position; `full`: the whole repository — a cold cache, the first sync of a repository after a restart, a log recreated under it). A delta p95 climbing is a node falling behind its pushes; a full sync's time is mostly its downloads, sixteen at once. |
| `crewlet.code.git.wait` | `ms` | `class` | How long a git process waited for a slot on this node, by `class` (`read`, `transfer`, `maintenance`). A p95 approaching ten seconds is a node about to answer clones and pushes with 503 — every slot of one lane busy for a whole read attempt. `transfer` waiting is a node serving as many clones and pushes as `git.max_transfers` admits (more git nodes, or more memory and a wider `git.max_transfers`); `read` waiting is a node out of `git.max_processes`, one core a slot. |
| `crewlet.code.git.cpu` | `ms` | `class` | CPU a git process tree spent, by lane: `transfer` is clones and pushes, `read` the cache's reads and a push's scans and fetch checks, `maintenance` the bitmaps, indexes and checks. One observation per process, its whole cost, recorded when it ends: its user and system time and that of every process it waited for (upload-pack's pack-objects, receive-pack's index-pack) — and for one the node ended (a deadline, a stall, a client gone) at least what its whole group had spent when it was signalled; on macOS, only what the process and the children it had reaped spent. So the sum is what a lane's runs cost, read over a window longer than the runs it counts — a clone may run for hours and a bitmap for a quarter of an hour, each landing whole in the window it ends in — and never the share of the node git is taking now, which is the container's own CPU usage. Read the sum and the count rather than the percentiles: a run past 64 s of CPU lands in the last bin. |
| `crewlet.code.push.duration` | `ms` | `outcome` | How long a git push took on this node, from its request to its answer, by `outcome` (`applied`, `pending`, `unknown`, `refused`, `failed`). `pending` growing is a code log whose records are durable and slow to apply here; `unknown` is a committer that stopped answering; the tail of `applied` is what a person waits for a push. |
| `crewlet.code.push.bytes` | `By` | — | The size of each push's bundle — the pack its receive-pack kept and the two indexes it wrote — observed once the pack is checked, whatever becomes of the push: the one object the object store stores for it, against `code.limits.max_push_bytes` (what the client may send) and the 1.25 GiB one push may store. |
| `crewlet.code.fetch.duration` | `ms` | `command`, `sync` | How long a fetch request took on this node, by `command` (`advertise`, `ls-refs`, `fetch`) and by what the cache had to do first (`sync`: `none`, `delta`, `full`). A `full` tail is cold caches downloading whole repositories; a `delta` tail is the barrier and the sync every answer that names a ref waits for. |
| `crewlet.code.host.spool.wait` | `ms` | `outcome` | How long each fetch counted by `crewlet.code.host.spool.waits` waited for room to spool, by the same `outcome` (`granted`, `expired`, `abandoned`; a `refused` one waited for nothing). The `granted` tail is what the wait adds to a checkout; one nearing 55 s is a node about to answer checkouts 503. |

## Gauges

A value that goes both ways, sampled at each export.

| Metric | Unit | Attributes | What it makes visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crewlet.statelog.drain.rows_per_second` | `1` | `domain` | The applier's observed drain, which every retry hint divides by. Seeded from a benchmark and then measured, so a hint on real hardware stops being an extrapolation from somebody else's. |
| `crewlet.statelog.drain.commits_per_second` | `1` | `domain` | Commits per second, which is the fsync rate under `synchronous = FULL` and the number a device budget is spent by. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.lag.seq` | `1` | `domain` | How many records this node is behind the log's head. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.lag.seconds` | `s` | `domain` | How OLD the oldest unapplied record is. Seconds are what a stall grace, a pending outcome and a copy taken out of service all turn on; sequences are not, and a lag of 4 000 says nothing about whether anything is wrong. |
| `crewlet.statelog.applied_through` | `1` | `domain` | The prefix this node has actually applied, which is lower than its checkpoint whenever a record was retained. |
| `crewlet.statelog.deferred.count` | `1` | `domain` | Records this build could not read and kept. Non-zero is a rolling upgrade in progress; non-zero and not falling is one that stopped. |
| `crewlet.statelog.deferred.oldest_age_seconds` | `s` | `domain` | How long the oldest retained record has been retained, which is what decides whether this node's copy stays in service. |
| `crewlet.statelog.waiters` | `1` | `domain` | Callers blocked on the applier right now. It is the depth of the queue a slow apply is making. |
| `crewlet.statelog.log.bytes` | `By` | `domain` | What the log actually holds, against its ceiling below. |
| `crewlet.statelog.log.max_bytes` | `By` | `domain` | The ceiling, read from the running stream rather than from this node's own configuration — the two differ, and the running one is what refuses the append. |
| `crewlet.statelog.log.headroom_fraction` | `1` | `domain` | How much of the ceiling ordinary writes are held to is left — on a log that claims identity, the ceiling less the gate reserve kept above it for evictions. At zero the log refuses every write AND every linearizable read, and the remedy is a fleet-wide maintenance cycle, so this is the one number worth alarming on long before it is small. |
| `crewlet.statelog.trim.blocked_seconds` | `s` | `domain`, `term` | How long one retention term has held the trim, named. A trim blocked for weeks is a log walking toward its ceiling with a cause an operator can act on. |
| `crewlet.backup.age` | `s` | — | How long ago the newest COMPLETE backup finished, read from the manifests on disk rather than from a counter this process keeps. A counter records that a process believed it took a backup; the disk records that one exists, and they differ in exactly the cases the alarm is for — a copy deleted, a volume never mounted, a schedule pointing at a path nobody ships from. A node holding no manifest reports NO SERIES rather than a value: zero is the freshest backup imaginable and every other number is an age nobody measured, so neither can stand for an absence. The absence is what the `backup_age` alarm says in words, and an `absent()` rule over this gauge is what a collector alerts on. |
| `crewlet.backup.holds` | `1` | — | Live trim holds. A pin that outlives its owner stops the trim until the stale bound expires it, so a count that does not return to zero is a backup that crashed mid-copy. |
| `crewlet.store.wal.bytes` | `By` | `file` | A write-ahead log a checkpoint cannot pass grows, and this is the only way to see it before the volume fills. |
| `crewlet.store.bytes` | `By` | `file` | The store's size on disk, which the snapshot's free-space precondition and the provisioning rule are both derived from. |
| `crewlet.tracker.search.concurrency` | `1` | — | Searches in flight, which is the row of the supported-corpus table this node is actually on: inside the one-second budget, about 345 000 sources with one running and about 136 000 with eight through the full scan, and about 545 000 and 183 000 through an index probing half its lists. |
| `crewlet.tracker.vector.coverage` | `1` | — | The fraction of sources carrying a current vector. It is how a stalled embedding backlog is reported, since it never drops a seat. |
| `crewlet.objects.s3.gate.limit` | `1` | — | How many attempts this node's S3 client lets its bucket hold at once while a throttle holds it back — seven tenths of the most the node had out at once when the bucket last throttled it, one more each round of answers — and zero while nothing does: the gate lifts a minute after the bucket's last throttle. Above zero for long is a fleet held over the prefix's rate; every request of the node — git syncs, the collector, backups, people's files — shares what it allows. |
| `crewlet.objects.s3.gate.waiting` | `1` | — | Attempts of this node's S3 client waiting in line for the gate, first come first served: what a throttle is costing the node now. High while `crewlet.objects.s3.gate.limit` stays low is a node sending more than the prefix will take from it — its requests wait rather than fail, until their own deadlines. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.bytes` | `By` | — | What this node's git cache holds on disk — every repository's packs, indexes and refs, plus the downloads and pushes in flight — against its byte budget, which it is evicted to, least recently used first, and for no other reason. Sitting at the budget is a cache doing its job; held above it is a repository larger than the budget being served, evicted once nothing reads it; climbing past it while syncs keep starting cold is a budget too small for the repositories this node serves. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.maintenance.refused` | `1` | `step` | Repositories this node's git cache cannot write a bitmap (`step` `bitmap`) or a commit-graph (`graph`) of now, because one needs more memory than the node can give its background work — as its latest pass found them. Each refused a bitmap is indexed without one; each refused a commit-graph walks its history by date, so a push of a commit dated before its parent walks every commit — slower, never refused. Either above zero raises code_maintenance_refused, since a repository refused its graph is refused its bitmap too; falling back is a repository purged, evicted or rebuilt smaller, or a node given more memory, which the cache reads again every ten seconds. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.repos` | `1` | — | Repositories with a cache on this node. One leaves when its rows are purged or the budget evicts it; every one that arrives cost a cold sync of the whole repository. Falling while the cache's bytes stay at the budget is eviction churn: every repository it drops is a cold sync the next time it is fetched. |
| `crewlet.code.git.processes` | `1` | `class` | Git processes running on this node, by `class`. `transfer` pinned at `git.max_transfers` while `crewlet.code.git.wait` climbs is a node serving as many clones and pushes as its memory was sized for; `maintenance` is background index rebuilding, at most half of `git.max_processes`. |
| `crewlet.code.git.lent_cores` | `1` | — | Cores of this node's read lane lent right now to pushes as extra index-pack threads — up to three a push, never the last free core. A loan is made when a push's receive-pack starts — the one that receives its pack, never the refs advertisement its first request is answered with — and repaid once its pack is indexed, so it covers the client's whole upload: lent cores held high while `crewlet.code.git.processes` for `read` sits low is slow uploads holding loans, and the reason a later push on this node indexes on one core. |
| `crewlet.alarm.active` | `1` | `kind` | Whether each named alarm is firing right now, 0 or 1. It is the same table the operator record renders and the CLI exits non-zero on, so a collector and a person see one answer. |

## Counters

Only ever rises. Rates and totals are your collector's arithmetic, never this engine's.

| Metric | Unit | Attributes | What it makes visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.outcomes` | `1` | `domain`, `outcome` | The three-valued write outcome, counted, and only the three — a refusal is on `publish.refusals` instead, because it says the write never happened at all. `unknown` is the one that matters most and had no counter: a broker flapping into ambiguity was visible only to the model that received the answer. |
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.conflicts` | `1` | `domain`, `subject_kind` | Writes that spent their whole round budget losing races on one subject, BY KIND. The refusal counter beside it says a conflict happened and not what it was about, and the remedy differs entirely: one contended object is a design question and a contended kind is a hot subject. |
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.rejections` | `1` | `domain`, `subject_kind` | How often a write loses a race, per kind of subject. It is what says whether a counter, a rank order or an ordinary object is the contended one. |
| `crewlet.statelog.publish.refusals` | `1` | `domain`, `reason` | Writes refused before or instead of an append, by `reason`, and EVERY value it carries is here, each with its remedy. The node: `evicted` (this node is removed from the fleet — run the write on another), `deferred` (it holds a record it cannot decode — a newer build serves it), `behind` (it has not applied a position the write needs — clears on its own), `below_floor` (it is below the log and must adopt a snapshot — another node writes meanwhile), `floor_unknown` (the floor or the log's ends could not be read — clears when coordination answers). The log: `log_full` (at its ceiling — raise it or unblock the trim), `skew` (a store and a stream restored out of step — restore both from one backup), `wrong_stream` (not the log this node's rows came from: rebuilt, ending below its checkpoint, holding another record there, or re-anchored past it by a peer — re-anchor, or adopt where a peer holds the generation), `log_truncated` (it lost records a peer's rows hold — settle which history the fleet keeps). The object: `deleted` (a permanent deletion marker — nothing recreates it). The operation: `op_reused` (its id names a record on another object) and `superseded` (its record landed and a later one undid it) — both answered by a NEW operation under a fresh id, never by a retry. A record that landed and a gate dropped is counted under the gate that dropped it — `evicted`, `deleted`, `abandoned` (written in a generation a reanchor abandoned) or `overtaken` (written after a restored reanchor, below its generation) — and is never re-decided, because republishing makes another record nothing applies. Such a record holds its operation id for the log's duplicate window, so the same id sent inside it, by any node, is collapsed onto the record and refused the same way: the write is retried under a fresh id, or under the same one once the window has passed. Beside the refusals: `conflict` for a write that lost every round, `exists` for a create whose object already exists, and `error` for a write that failed before it could answer. A refusal is not one of the three outcomes: it says the write never happened, and each reason has a different remedy, so one counter with an outcome dimension would hide them all. |
| `crewlet.statelog.read.refusals` | `1` | `domain`, `level`, `code` | Every refusal code, counted. The codes, each with its own remedy, had no counter between them, so an operator had no rejection rate for any of them. |
| `crewlet.statelog.read.served` | `1` | `domain`, `level` | Reads answered per level, which is the denominator every refusal fraction needs and the check on the assumed read rate the log's own size is derived from. |
| `crewlet.statelog.barrier.appends` | `1` | `domain` | Barrier records appended. Against reads served it is the single-flight ratio, which says whether coalescing is doing anything at all. |
| `crewlet.statelog.barrier.applied` | `1` | `domain`, `stream` | Barrier records applied from each log — every node's linearizable reads on it, since every node applies every record. It is the rate `census_drift` holds against the census, per log: a node's own appends are only its share of the fleet's reads, and on a fleet of several serving nodes they describe a company that many times quieter than it is. The alarm's 24-hour window files each barrier at the hour the broker stored it, so a node replaying a backlog does not read days of reads as one; this cumulative series counts them as they are applied, so it jumps by a backlog's barriers when one is replayed. |
| `crewlet.statelog.linger.yields` | `1` | `domain` | How often a waiter cut a batch short. It is the batching the applier gives up to answer a read promptly, and without it that trade is invisible. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.records` | `1` | `domain`, `result` | Records consumed, by what happened to them: applied, retained, gated, skipped, or reprocessed by a build that could read what an earlier one retained — a retained record a gate drops when it is reprocessed is counted `gated`, as it would have been live, since it wrote no row. A node applying nothing while its position advances is healthy on lag alone. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.retries` | `1` | `domain` | Attempts the apply loop retried in place after a failure that was not a stop — a fetch the broker did not answer, a transaction the disk refused, an applier that errored. A rate that stays up past the retry budget is a node whose rows have stopped moving, and its health says so. |
| `crewlet.statelog.apply.tx.aborts` | `1` | `domain` | Apply transactions whose body the store ran more than once, because an attempt failed transiently after it began. It reads zero by construction: this database detects write conflicts per file, so every write transaction takes the file's lock at its BEGIN and queues for it, and no commit elsewhere in the file can abort an apply. A non-zero count on the operator's own hardware means the retry budget is being spent rather than held in reserve. |
| `crewlet.statelog.records_gated` | `1` | `gate`, `subject_kind` | Records an apply gate dropped, by the gate that dropped each — the domain's own (`evicted`, `deleted`) or the framework's (`abandoned`, `overtaken`). Each node counts a record once, where its own applier drops it, when the transaction that drops it commits — never once per attempt at that transaction. A write refused because its record — or another node's copy it was collapsed onto — was dropped is a refusal, counted under `crewlet.statelog.publish.refusals`, and not a second drop. A dropped commit is recoverable by nothing, and this is the only place anyone would see that it happened. |
| `crewlet.statelog.anchors.swept` | `1` | `domain` | Arbitration anchors this node's applier removed under the trim's `trimmed` records (ADR-0032), counted once the transaction that removed them commits. Every node applies every record, so every data node counts the same removals. Flat is the normal reading of a log whose purged objects all wrote again later — their anchors moved above the trim and nothing is below it to remove; a sweep that is failing shows as a `retention_anchor_sweep_failed` line from the trim's holder, and as anchors below the log's first record that keep growing while this stays flat. |
| `crewlet.history.answers` | `1` | `question`, `coverage` | What each fleet history read covered: `complete` when every live node answered inside the fleet read budget, `partial` when one did not. Turn-level detail lives only on the node that published it, so a partial answer is missing that node's rows — and the history_partial alarm is a fraction of this counter. |
| `crewlet.tracker.search.answers` | `1` | `coverage`, `semantic` | What each answer actually covered: whether every bucket of the corpus was scanned, and whether the semantic half ran (`full`), was asked for and lost (`skipped`), or was never asked for (`off` — a keyword search, or a company with no embeddings). Both alarms below it are a FRACTION of this counter, and a short answer is indistinguishable from a short corpus without it. |
| `crewlet.tracker.feed.unreadable` | `1` | `source` | Change records this build could not translate into a wake. Both domain consumers are deliberately uncapped, so such a record is never dropped — it redelivers for ever at the head of the consumer with every wake behind it waiting, which has no other symptom at all. |
| `crewlet.tracker.bulk.calls` | `1` | `result` | How often a bulk edit is issued, by `result`: `admitted` under the fleet's bulk lease, `refused` because another is applying, and `fail_open` — let through with NO lease, because the coordination store did not answer the admission or the mixed-version gate refused it. The refusal arithmetic rested on an assumed ten a day, a number with no counter behind it; this is that number. A `fail_open` is a bulk the fleet-wide bound did not cover, and counted as `admitted` it left no trace: a store that refused every admission looked exactly like a fleet whose bulks never collided. |
| `crewlet.tracker.bulk.apply_seconds` | `s` | — | Seconds of applier occupancy bulk edits projected, summed. Over 24 hours it IS the fleet-wide read-degradation budget: every second here is a second in which reads are behind and writes are pending on every node. |
| `crewlet.objects.s3.attempts` | `1` | `operation`, `outcome` | Every attempt this node's S3 client sent its bucket, by S3 `operation` (the API's own name: `HeadBucket`, `HeadObject`, `GetObject`, `PutObject`, `CreateMultipartUpload`, `UploadPart`, `CompleteMultipartUpload`, `AbortMultipartUpload`, `DeleteObject`, `DeleteObjects`, `ListObjectsV2`, `ListMultipartUploads`, and S3 Express's `CreateSession`) and what the bucket made of it (`outcome`): `answered` — served, a success or a refusal such as a missing key; `throttled` — asked to slow down (`503 SlowDown`, any `429`, MinIO's `SlowDownRead` and `SlowDownWrite`), which cuts the node's gate; `failed` — any other answer: a server error that is no throttle, or a status no request expects, such as a redirect to another region; `unreached` — no answer at all: a connection refused or reset, a name that did not resolve, a TLS failure, or an attempt never sent because its S3 Express session could not be had; `stalled` — the bucket stopped moving the attempt for a minute: took no more of its body, acknowledged none of it at the node's socket and sent none of its answer, so the request was given up; `ended` — the attempt's own deadline or its caller ended it in flight. An operation's RETRIES are this counter's total for it, less the count of `crewlet.objects.s3.request.attempts` for it, plus that histogram's `unsent` count for it. `throttled` rising is the fleet over the bucket's rate for the prefix (S3 serves 5 500 reads and 3 500 writes a second a prefix); `failed` the bucket's own fault; `unreached` the network or the endpoint. |
| `crewlet.code.commit.busy` | `1` | — | Pushes refused `busy`, undecided — the client runs `git push` again — for one of three causes that point at different remedies. A BACKLOG: a repository taking pushes faster than one node's committer commits them (its queue of 1 024 pushes, or sixteen records' bytes, is full), or the node holding sixty-four records' bytes of pushes across its repositories. A DEADLINE, either way round: a push that waited behind earlier ones until its asker's attempt had no more left than the 30-second commit budget and a second for the answer, or one that ARRIVED with no more than that left — the attempt spent before it reached the committer, waiting for the node to take it (its proposal slots full), for the node to reach the asker's own writes, or under a caller deadline shorter than 31 seconds; asked with no deadline, a push that waited that budget whole. Or a record that lost every compare-and-set round it may take. No repository is an attribute — which one is hot is a question for its rows, not a time series a repository. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.adoptions` | `1` | `outcome` | Pushes this node's git cache was asked to adopt — the pack the push's receive-pack wrote, linked into the cache once its row applied rather than downloaded back by the node that took the push — by `outcome`. `adopted`: linked in by the adoption itself. `handed`: a sync or a verify was writing the repository's directory, and the adoption left the pack to it, staged; it installs the pack from that staging rather than the object store before it lets the directory go, unless it had already begun to download it. `held`: the cache already held the pack. `uncached`: the repository's cache left this node between the push's sync and its adoption — the repository purged — so there was nothing to adopt into. `failed`: the links failed, and the next sync downloads the pack, one GET of its bundle; rising, it is this node's disk refusing writes. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.checks` | `1` | `file`, `outcome`, `trigger` | Files of this node's git cache held to their own checksum — the trailer git writes at the end of every pack and index file, the SHA-1 of the bytes before it — because git checks none of them when it reads: a damaged index file can answer wrong without a word, and a damaged pack is sent to clients byte for byte. Before a copy this process did not write answers its first request, every index file it holds; and behind the serving, a SCRUB of every file a copy holds, packs included — once after a copy a previous process left first answers, daily while it is used, and at once when a git process over it reports a pack it could not read or crashes; and when a request fails on a pack or an object, every index file again, whatever was checked before, then every file if that repaired nothing. By `file` (`commit-graph`, `multi-pack-index`, `bitmap`, `midx-rev`: files the node derives from its packs; `idx`, `rev`: a pack's index and reverse index, stored with its push; `pack`, the pack itself, read only by a scrub), `outcome` (`sound`; `damaged` — a derived file dropped to be written again, a stored one fetched again with its pack, one download; `unreadable`, a read of it that failed — repaired as though damaged, since a file the disk cannot read is one git cannot serve, and never a refused read slot or an ended request, which decide nothing and are not counted; `replaced`, the file renamed over or removed while it was read, so no verdict is its) and `trigger` (`first`, a copy's first full sync in this process, which reads every index file a previous process left, or the scrub after it, which reads every pack and every file that sync did not; `unvouched`, a later full sync reading only what this process has neither written nor checked since; `scrub`, a used copy's daily scrub; `report`, a scrub a git process's report or crash made due; `forced`, the in-place repair a request's pack or object failure asks first, every index file held to its checksum whatever was checked before; `request`, the scrub that repair runs at once when it found nothing, and a pack a git process named in words, confirmed against its row and fetched again). Any `damaged` is a disk losing data, or something outside the engine writing into the cache: the copy repairs it, and a verify of the repository names what else that disk holds damaged. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.reports` | `1` | `part`, `outcome` | Damage any git process over this node's git cache named — whether its request failed or git read around the damage and answered — as the cache took it, by the `part` named (`commit-graph`, `multi-pack-index`, `chunk`: a derived file of either, dropped by a repair round with no request waiting and written again at once; `pack`, `object`: stored damage, and `hint`, a pack git named in words alone, each making the copy's scrub due at once, which holds every file it holds to its checksum and fetches again what fails; `crash`, a git process dying of a signal the node did not send — what a damaged reverse index or bitmap does to a clone, naming nothing — which makes the scrub due the same way; any of these four named by the git a request ran, which repairs what that git fails with before its first byte, is held for that request until it asks its repair or lets the copy go, and counted then) and its `outcome`: `queued`, a repair asked — a round, or the scrub; `deferred`, asked while a check of the repository ran, repaired once it ends; `stale`, not dropped — the node wrote the file after the process that named it began, so the report was of the file it replaced — and, for a `pack` or an `object`, a failed request whose process began before the node last wrote a repair into the copy, answered from the copy as it stands once no round is repairing it and run once more rather than repaired further; `unrouted`, a pack, an object or a hint named by a push's own throwaway repository, which may be the client's pack; `again`, a derived file named damaged within a day of its last drop for damage, whatever the node wrote of it between: dropped and left to the ordinary schedule rather than written again at once; `cooldown`, a stored report or a crash within an hour of a scrub of the copy that found nothing, which makes no other; `covered`, one within an hour of a scrub whose findings still wait for their repair, which is its answer; `request`, one held for the request whose git named it and answered by the repair that request asked — its in-place round, its scrub and, past both, its rebuild — with no scrub of the copy made due beside it (one the request did not repair — it failed past its first byte, failed in a way the node does not repair, or never failed — is counted under the others as the request lets the copy go). `queued` rising is a disk losing data under the cache; `again`, a disk that keeps losing it; `cooldown` rising, a git process failing on something the copy's checksums do not show; `request` rising, requests failing on damage they had repaired under them. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.hints` | `1` | `outcome` | Packs of this node's git cache that a git process named as holding a corrupt object in words alone — git 2.56 and later report a packed object's damage through a bare message, which nothing reads as damage — one a naming, by the verdict that answered it (`outcome`): `confirmed`, the pack's bytes are not its row's and the repository is rebuilt (counted under `crewlet.code.cache.rebuilds{reason=corrupt}`); `sound`, its bytes are the row's and nothing is repaired; `unknown`, no row names the pack at the log's head; `unread`, no verdict — the rows or the pack could not be read in time, or its files moved under the hash; `gone`, the request left before the verdict, the hash going on for the next. `confirmed` rising is disk damage a verify of the repository names; `sound` rising is git naming damage the pack does not hold — a git bug, or a request that made git print the sentence — which costs one hash of the pack's files and never a rebuild; `unread` and `gone` rising is a node too busy or a disk too slow to decide a hash inside its bound. Beside `crewlet.code.cache.hint.hashes`, the namings one hash answered. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.hint.hashes` | `1` | `outcome` | Hashes of a pack of this node's git cache that git named corrupt in words alone (`crewlet.code.cache.hints`), by what each decided (`outcome`): `confirmed`, `sound`, `unknown` and `unread`, as there. One a pack's files however many namings wait on it — a naming of a pack being hashed waits for that hash, and a verdict is kept for as long as the pack's files are the ones it was reached on — each run on the cache's own time rather than a request's, a read slot a 64 MiB piece, and bounded by the hash alone. Namings less hashes is what waiting saved; `unread` here is a hash the node could not fit, which the next naming starts again. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.maintenance.refusals` | `1` | `reason`, `step` | Steps of the background work on a repository this node's git cache found it will not run, counted once for each copy of a repository the cache holds and each step, by `reason` and `step`. `memory`: the step's charge — its own figure an object of the repository, and 240 more for room beside it for a clone of the repository — is more than this node can give its background work, which is its memory (its cgroup's limit where one is set) less what it keeps for its git lanes, the store, the broker and the engine. `bitmap` (1000 bytes an object): the repository is indexed without one, and a clone walks its history; `index` (80): it is served from its packs' own indexes, a round's index included; `graph` (56): its walks go by date, and a push of a commit dated before its parent walks every commit. Slower, never wrong. Rising is repositories outgrowing the node; the code_maintenance_refused alarm stands while any bitmap is refused. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.rebuild.refusals` | `1` | `reason`, `rule` | Rebuilds this node's git cache refused, by the `reason` the git process gave (`corrupt`, `missing` or `shape` — a shape only once reading the directory whole in place left the pool still refusing it, since that repair downloads nothing and is never refused) and the `rule` that refused it. `unchanged`: the repository's cache holds exactly what a rebuild that did not end the failure read less than a day ago, and nothing has written into it since, so another would make the same directory — never for `shape`, whose refusal is itself something written into it; `cooldown`: the last attempt began too recently — ten minutes after the first of a line of attempts that keep failing, twice as long after each one after it, at most a day, a line starting again once a day passes with no rebuild asked for. Each refusal fails the request that asked at once rather than downloading the whole repository again. Rising at all is damage no rebuild repairs — a pack the object store lost or holds damaged, rows naming an object no pack holds, a directory something keeps writing into — which a verify of the repository names; flat while `crewlet.code.cache.rebuilds` rises is damage each rebuild ended. |
| `crewlet.code.cache.rebuilds` | `1` | `reason` | Repositories this node's git cache read whole from the rows again, by `reason`. `corrupt`, `derived`, `missing` and `shape` are a repair a git process asked for — a request's or a sync's own — read from the format strings of git's own reports, which no request can write. `corrupt` and `missing` are a rebuild into a new directory beside the damaged one: it found a pack or an index it could not read, or an object a row names that no pack held — the last step of a request's repair, after an in-place repair and a scrub of every file the copy holds found nothing to fetch again, so it links every pack the scrub found whole and downloads only the rest, nothing at all when the damage is in the rows; a sync's own git that names such damage asks it directly. `derived` is a damaged derived file (the multi-pack-index with its bitmap and reverse index, the commit-graph, or a chunk-format file of either), named by any git process over the copy and repaired IN PLACE — the same directory read whole again, the files the damage named DROPPED so the round or the maintainer rewrites sound ones over the same packs, none downloaded — since those are derived files, not the repository; damage the drop does not end escalates to `corrupt`; a request's pack or object failure whose in-place repair only dropped derived files is counted `derived` too. `shape` is the pool refusing to run git there because the directory is not the shape the engine writes (its config edited, a commondir, an objects directory not its own, or an alternates file planted in it), repaired IN PLACE — the same directory read whole again, every pack it holds reused and none downloaded — and rebuilt into a new one only when the pool still refuses it after that; any of them rising is disk or object-store damage, or something outside the engine writing into the cache, which a verify of the repository names — every pack checked against its row, the ref file against the digest written with it, the directory's shape, and git's connectivity check. `verify` is that check, asked to repair what it found: read whole IN PLACE, as `shape` is, where everything it found is the copy's own directory out of place — a file or entry the engine does not write there, a pack no row names, its shape — every pack, index, bitmap and graph kept and none downloaded; rebuilt into a new directory otherwise, or for what that read leaves — a shape written past its sweep included, never counted under `shape` — each counted once it has read the copy whole, so a read in place that shape stopped is not. `stored` is no read of the rows' history at all: a pack whose stored files — the pack, its index or its reverse index — a check before serving or a scrub behind it found failing their own checksum, a full sync found at another size than their row's, a request's repair found the copy had lost, or a git process named in words and its row confirmed, fetched again IN PLACE with one download a pack, renamed over the damaged files, counted once a sync that did it — the first repair of a request's pack or object failure, which reaches `corrupt` or `missing` only when it and a scrub find nothing; rising is a disk losing data under the cache. `stream` is the code log RECREATED under the cache (provisioned anew, its stamp not the one the cache read under); `rewound` is the log gone BACK under it on the same stream — a broker restored from an older copy — seen in a read at the log's head below a position the cache had read. Either of those counts every repository on the node once, as its next sync converges to the rows the log holds rather than taking a delta from a position that log never had or has since given to other records. A repository marked to be read whole for more than one reason at once is read once and counted once, under the first: damaged derived files found on a copy already marked for its shape or for the log are counted under that reason, dropped all the same (logged `code_cache_derived_repaired`). |
| `crewlet.code.host.spool.waits` | `1` | `outcome` | Fetch requests large enough to spool — a partial clone's lazy fetch past a mebibyte of wants — that could not start spooling, or take room for the rest of their body, at once on this node and waited their turn, by `outcome`: `granted`, served after its wait; `expired`, answered 503 after waiting 55 s unserved; `abandoned`, its request ended while it waited; and `refused`, answered 503 at once because it had to wait and found no place to — the node's waiting room full, four places a git transfer slot, or its credential's quarter of it, a lane's width. git does not retry a lazy fetch, so every `expired` or `refused` is a checkout that failed, and git prints only the status: the `code_fetch_spool_unserved` line names the token and what held it back. `granted` climbing is a credential at its quarter of the node's spooling — one token behind several CI runners, which a token per runner ends — or a node whose spooling is full: more git transfer slots (more memory, a wider `git.max_transfers`) or more git nodes. |

## What is deliberately not here

**Rates.** Every counter is a monotonic total and your collector divides. A
rate computed in this process would be a rate over a window nobody chose,
disagreeing with the one on your dashboard.

**A `/metrics` route.** OTLP reaches Prometheus through the collector you
already run for traces. A second wire format would be a second thing to
authenticate on an API whose guard and whose exemptions are both load-bearing.

**Per-object series.** See the attribute rule above.
